issues.legal_issue: A court deciding whether eviction for a landlord’s bona fide requirement would cause greater hardship to the tenant must weigh the circumstances of both landlord and tenant, including alternative accommodation and their practical ability to obtain it.
material_facts: The landlord had established a bona fide need for the premises to start a business and had substantial business experience and the means to carry it on.
The tenant was not in actual possession; another person occupied the premises, had a separate shop, and used the premises as a godown.
The tenant was aged and infirm, and the occupant paid him a regular amount for maintenance.
The courts below found no greater hardship to the tenant, while the High Court reached the opposite conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to find that eviction would cause greater hardship to the tenant; the eviction decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 13(1)(g) and 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the court must balance the hardship eviction would cause against the hardship refusal would cause. Relevant considerations include alternative accommodation, the parties’ financial means to obtain accommodation, and the nature and extent of their business or residential needs. Alternative accommodation is important but not decisive, and the question depends on the circumstances of each case. The Court referred to the analogous provision considered in Sims v. Wilson, Fowle v. Bell, Smith v. Penny, Chandler v. Strevett, and Kelly v. Goodwin.

rule.if: eviction_case_based_on_landlord_business_need and landlord_has_bona_fide_need and landlord_has_business_experience_and_means and tenant_is_not_in_actual_possession and occupier_has_separate_business_premises and occupier_uses_premises_for_storage

predicates.eviction_case_based_on_landlord_business: The proceeding seeks eviction so the landlord can use the premises for the landlord’s business.
predicates.landlord_has_bona_fide_need: The landlord has established a genuine need to use the premises.
predicates.landlord_has_business_experience_and_mea: The landlord has relevant business experience and the means to carry on the proposed business.
predicates.tenant_is_not_in_actual_possession: The tenant has parted with actual possession of the premises.
predicates.occupier_has_separate_business_premises: The person occupying the premises has separate premises from which to conduct that person’s business.
predicates.occupier_uses_premises_for_storage: The person occupying the premises uses them to store goods rather than to conduct the person’s business there.

issues.definition: When a landlord establishes a bona fide business need and the tenant has parted with possession to an occupier who has separate business premises and uses the disputed premises only for storage, an eviction decree should be passed where the landlord also has the experience and means to pursue the business.

issues.legal_issue: In comparing hardship between a landlord and tenant, hardship to a complete stranger occupying the premises is not a relevant party’s hardship.
material_facts: The tenant had placed another person in occupation of the premises.
That person had a separate shop and used the premises as a godown.
The High Court relied on the tenant’s dependence on payments from that occupier when finding greater hardship to the tenant.
issues.conclusion: The court must consider the hardship of the landlord and tenant, not that of a complete stranger; the High Court erred in relying on the arrangement with the occupier to find greater hardship to the tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2) requires comparison of hardship to the landlord and tenant. It does not permit the court to treat hardship to a complete stranger as hardship to either of them.

predicates.rent_eviction_case_with_comparative_hard: The proceeding concerns eviction in which the court must compare hardship to landlord and tenant.
predicates.premises_occupied_by_nonparty: A person other than the landlord or tenant occupies the premises.
predicates.hardship_claim_rests_on_nonparty_occupan: A party’s claimed hardship depends on the circumstances of the nonparty occupier.

issues.definition: In a rent eviction proceeding requiring a comparison of the landlord’s and tenant’s hardship, hardship attributed to a nonparty occupier is not counted when that occupier’s circumstances are the basis of the claim.

issues.legal_issue: The comparative-hardship decision cannot turn merely on the burden of proof; both parties must lead evidence relevant to the balance.
material_facts: The tenant pleaded that eviction would cause greater hardship because it would disrupt his business and affect his livelihood.
The landlord relied on his displacement, business experience, and need to use the premises for business.
The dispute required the court to compare the circumstances of both sides.
issues.conclusion: The comparative-hardship decision cannot be resolved merely by assigning the burden of proof to the tenant; both parties must lead evidence.
issues.legal_principle: On the language of section 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the question of greater hardship depends on the facts and circumstances of the case, and both parties must lead evidence. The Court distinguished the English approach, under which the burden had been placed on the tenant, while referring to Sims v. Wilson, Fowle v. Bell, Smith v. Penny, Chandler v. Strevett, and Kelly v. Goodwin as decisions interpreting an analogous provision.

predicates.rent_eviction_case_requiring_comparative: The proceeding requires a court to decide whether eviction would cause greater hardship than refusing eviction.

issues.definition: When a rent eviction proceeding requires comparative-hardship assessment, both landlord and tenant must lead evidence relevant to that assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising statutory revisional jurisdiction may not replace lower courts’ findings by reappraising evidence when those findings are not perverse or erroneous.
material_facts: The courts below found that the tenant was not in actual possession and that the occupier used the premises as a godown while having a separate shop.
The High Court reached a different comparative-hardship conclusion after considering the evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the lower courts had applied their minds and that their finding was not manifestly perverse or erroneous.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not substitute its finding for that of the courts below by reappraising the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as substituted by Gujarat Act 18 of 1965, the High Court’s revisional jurisdiction is wider than its jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but is limited to satisfying itself that the decision is according to law. It cannot replace a lower court’s finding on reappraisal when that finding is not perverse or erroneous.

predicates.statutory_rent_revision: The matter is before a High Court in revision under a rent-control statute.
predicates.lower_court_finding_is_not_perverse_or_e: The lower court’s finding is neither perverse nor erroneous.
predicates.proposed_interference_reappraises_eviden: The proposed intervention would replace the lower court’s finding through a fresh assessment of the evidence.

issues.definition: In a statutory rent revision, if the lower court’s finding is not perverse or erroneous and intervention would reappraise evidence, the High Court must not substitute its own finding.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s comparative-hardship claim does not remain for decision after the tenant dies during the appeal.
material_facts: The tenant died while the appeal was pending.
The dispute included whether eviction would cause greater hardship to the tenant.
issues.conclusion: After the tenant’s death during the appeal, the question of greater hardship to that tenant did not arise.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the tenant’s death during the appeal meant that the question of greater hardship to that tenant under section 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, no longer arose.

predicates.rent_eviction_appeal_with_tenant_compara: An appeal in a rent eviction proceeding includes an issue about hardship to the tenant.
predicates.tenant_dies_during_appeal: The tenant dies while the appeal is pending.

issues.definition: When a tenant dies during an appeal that includes a comparative-hardship issue about that tenant, the tenant’s hardship issue no longer arises.
